c.tagline: Where the Río de la Plata meets laid-back South America.

taxi.color: black with a yellow checkered stripe
taxi.fareNote: Fares rise at night (10pm-6am), on Sundays and holidays; small surcharges apply for extra luggage and airport pickups.

emergency.medical: 911 (unified emergency dispatch; private ambulance memberships like SUAT/UCM are common locally)
emergency.note: 911 is Uruguay's national unified number for police, fire and medical emergencies.

avoid.reason: Caution in Ciudad Vieja after dark and around the port; some peripheral barrios (Casavalle, Cerro) higher-crime

hood_desc: Montevideo's historic old town on the peninsula, packed with colonial-era buildings, the Mercado del Puerto and late-night bars; best for first-time visitors who want to walk to major sights, museums and nightlife.

The bustling downtown core around Plaza Independencia, Avenida 18 de Julio and the Palacio Salvo, dense with hotels, shops, theaters and government buildings; suits business travelers and those who want transit and services right outside the door.

A leafy, upscale residential district built around its own sandy beach and rambla promenade, lined with cafés and apartment towers; ideal for travelers wanting a relaxed, local beach-town feel with easy bus access downtown.

A polished, walkable neighborhood anchored by a shopping mall built inside a former prison, close to the rambla and Parque Rodó; good for shoppers, families and anyone wanting quiet tree-lined streets near the coast.

A leafy garden suburb near the airport with mansions, a casino and quiet beaches; best for travelers with an early flight or those seeking a calm, embassy-district atmosphere away from downtown bustle.
lodging: Sofitel Montevideo Casino Carrasco and Spa

water.note: Tap water is treated to high standards and safe to drink.

sys.n: STM city buses (CUTCSA and other operators)

transit.pay: Fares are tapped with a rechargeable Tarjeta STM (Tarjeta Común) card sold at kiosks and topped up with cash, giving a discounted per-ride fare; riders without a card can pay a higher cash fare directly to the driver.
transit.hours: Most routes run roughly 5-6 AM to midnight, with a reduced network of night ('nocturno') buses on select lines in the early hours on weekends.
transit.note: Montevideo has no metro, subway or tram; city buses coordinated under the Sistema de Transporte Metropolitano (STM) are the backbone of public transit, supplemented by taxis and rideshare apps.

bus: Tres Cruces Bus Terminal (intercity and international coaches)
ferry: Buquebus and Colonia Express ferries to Buenos Aires, Argentina, from the Terminal Fluvio-Marítima near Ciudad Vieja

transit.m: CA1 city bus to Tres Cruces/downtown (~45-60 min)

tip.r: A tip of around 10% is appreciated at restaurants when not already included, but is not obligatory; rounding up is customary for taxis and casual services.

food.name: Chivito
food.desc: Uruguay's national sandwich: thin grilled steak with ham, mozzarella, tomato, lettuce, olives, mayo and often a fried egg, with chips.

places.name: Expreso Pocitos
places.note: Neighbourhood bar widely named for one of the best chivitos in town.

places.name: Bar Arocena
places.note: Classic corner bar that locals cite for a proper old-school chivito.

places.name: La Pasiva
places.note: City institution; chivito with its famous house mustard.

food.name: Asado
food.desc: Beef ribs, sausage and morcilla grilled slowly over wood embers and eaten in stages with chimichurri. A weekend-long social ritual.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Hall of wood-fired grills that becomes a carnivore cathedral at noon.

places.name: La Pulperia
places.note: Unfussy parrilla packed with locals for unrivalled meat quality.

places.name: Mercado Ferrando
places.note: Modern market hall with a good grill and a younger local crowd.

food.name: Milanesa
food.desc: Breaded beef cutlet fried thin, served plain, a caballo with fried eggs, or napolitana with ham, tomato and melted cheese.

places.name: La Pasiva
places.note: Cheap, fast and everywhere; the default local milanesa stop.

places.name: Mercado Ferrando
places.note: Several counters do a modern take on the classic cutlet.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Long-running downtown parrilla with big, traditional portions.

food.name: Pizza and faina
food.desc: A slice of thick mozzarella pizza stacked with faina, a chickpea-flour flatbread, and eaten standing at the counter with a glass of wine.

places.name: Bar Tasende
places.note: Historic stand-up bar famous for pizza, faina and medio y medio.

places.name: La Pasiva
places.note: Reliable branch of the city chain for pizza-and-faina at any hour.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Counters around the grills sell faina to go with the meat.

food.name: Choripan and morcilla dulce
food.desc: Grilled chorizo in a crusty roll with chimichurri, plus Uruguay's sweet blood sausage studded with walnuts and orange peel.

places.name: Mercado del Puerto
places.note: Every grill serves chorizo and morcilla dulce straight off the coals.

places.name: Mercado Agricola de Montevideo
places.note: Restored market hall with parrilla counters and local producers.

places.name: Rambla weekend parrilla carts
places.note: Waterfront carts firing up chorizo for walkers and cyclists.

food.name: Alfajores
food.desc: Two soft biscuits sandwiching dulce de leche, rolled in coconut or coated in chocolate or meringue. The standard merienda sweet.

places.name: Alfajores del Uruguay Cafe
places.note: Cafe and shop devoted to artisanal Uruguayan alfajores.

places.name: Confiteria La Vienesa
places.note: Long-standing confiteria chain for pastries, breads and alfajores.

places.name: Mercado Agricola de Montevideo
places.note: Several artisan bakers sell boxed alfajores to take away.

food.name: Medio y medio
food.desc: Half still white wine, half sparkling, served very cold in a small glass. Invented in Montevideo and drunk with pizza or asado.

places.name: Bar Roldos
places.note: Serving medio y medio inside the market since 1886; the original.

places.name: Bar Tasende
places.note: Stand-up counter pairing medio y medio with pizza and faina.

places.name: Baar Fun Fun
places.note: Historic tango bar known for its sweet uvita and medio y medio.

food.name: Mate
food.desc: Yerba mate steeped in a gourd and sipped through a metal bombilla, refilled from a thermos under the arm. Uruguayans carry it everywhere.

places.name: Mercado Agricola de Montevideo
places.note: Stalls selling yerba, gourds and bombillas plus advice on curing them.

places.name: Rambla kiosks
places.note: Kiosks refill thermoses with hot water so you can drink like a local.

places.name: Ciudad Vieja mate shops
places.note: Old-town shops selling hand-made gourds and local yerba brands.

landmarks: Palacio Legislativo
This grand marble parliament building, completed in 1925, dazzles with neoclassical columns, sweeping staircases, and intricate mosaics inside Uruguay's seat of government.
Palacio Salvo
This eccentric Art Deco skyscraper towering over Plaza Independencia was once South America's tallest building and remains Montevideo's most recognizable silhouette.
Plaza Independencia
Montevideo's central square blends colonial and modern eras, anchored by the equestrian statue and mausoleum of national hero José Artigas beneath his tomb.
Ciudad Vieja (Old Town)
Cobblestone streets lined with faded colonial and Art Nouveau facades make this historic quarter a favorite spot for wandering, photography, and tango-filled evenings.
Rambla de Montevideo
Stretching over 20 kilometers along the Río de la Plata, this iconic waterfront promenade is where locals jog, sip mate, and watch spectacular sunsets.
Mercado del Puerto
This bustling 19th-century iron-framed market house is packed with lively parrilla grills, making it the go-to spot for sizzling Uruguayan barbecue and atmosphere.
Estadio Centenario
Built for the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, this legendary stadium and its Torre de los Homenajes remain a sacred pilgrimage site for football fans.
Teatro Solís
Uruguay's oldest and most prestigious theater dazzles with a lavish neoclassical interior of gold leaf and red velvet, hosting opera, ballet, and symphony performances.
Montevideo Sign
This giant colorful lettering installed on the Rambla near the port has become the city's ultimate selfie spot, symbolizing civic pride for visitors and locals alike.
Cerro de Montevideo and Fortress
Crowned by a historic lighthouse and fortress, this hill across the bay offers the classic panoramic postcard view of Montevideo's skyline and harbor.

train.note: Uruguay has no international passenger trains. Domestic rail is minimal - AFE runs only a limited commuter service out of Montevideo, so almost all intercity travel is by bus or ferry.

intl.to: Buenos Aires & Mendoza (Argentina), Porto Alegre & Florianópolis (Brazil), Asunción (Paraguay)

bus.note: International coaches leave from the Tres Cruces bus terminal. Bring your passport - border checks are handled during the trip. The Buenos Aires service usually runs overnight (about 8h).

ferry.note: Buquebus runs the direct fast ferry across the Río de la Plata from Montevideo's port to Buenos Aires (roughly 2h15 by high-speed craft, longer on the bus-plus-ferry option via Colonia). Rival lines Colonia Express and Seacat depart from Colonia, not Montevideo.
